result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.all_spanning_trees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Enumerate all spanning trees of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28235-L28399){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.all_spanning_trees( max_trees=None, weight_attr=None, return_subgraphs=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![All spanning trees](/assets/graphs/all-spanning-trees.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a triangle A, B, C with a pendant node D attached to C. Right: its three spanning trees, one per row; each keeps edge C–D and drops one triangle edge (drawn dashed), with the tree edges A–C B–C C–D, A–B B–C C–D, and A–B A–C C–D listed beside them." width="100%"} A spanning tree is a subgraph that connects all vertices with the minimum number of edges (`V-1` edges for `V` vertices) and contains no cycles. This method enumerates all possible spanning trees, which is useful for reliability analysis and network design. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_trees]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of spanning trees to return. If `None`, defaults to `1000` to prevent excessive memory usage. Set to a specific value for different limits. [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of edge attribute to use for weights in the returned edges. If `None` (default), uses the edge's weight field. If the attribute doesn't exist, defaults to `1.0`. [return_subgraphs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a list of Graph objects, each representing a spanning tree. If `False`, returns a list of edge lists (each edge is a (source, target, weight) tuple). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[Graph] or list[list[tuple[str, str, float]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Either a list of Graph objects or a list of edge lists, depending on the `return_subgraphs=` parameter. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is disconnected (no spanning tree exists) or empty. ::: ## Warnings {.doc-warnings} The number of spanning trees can be extremely large. For a complete graph `Kn`, there are `n^(n-2)` spanning trees (Cayley's formula). Use `max_trees=` to limit results. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} By Cayley's formula (1889) the complete graph $K_n$ has $n^{n - 2}$ spanning trees, and that combinatorial explosion is not confined to complete graphs: even mildly dense inputs produce tree counts that exceed available memory well before enumeration finishes. The implementation enumerates by systematic edge substitution starting from a base spanning tree, exchanging tree edges for non-tree edges in a controlled order that hits each distinct tree exactly once. The `max_trees=` cap (defaulting to $1000$) is a hard budget, not a hint; treat it as the guardrail it is. Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem lets you count spanning trees analytically as $\det(L^*)$ (a cofactor of the Laplacian) when you only need the *number* and not the enumeration itself. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Reliability Analysis: Finding Backup Paths** With one extra diagonal edge added to a 4-cycle, there's more than one way to pick 3 edges that connect all 4 nodes without a cycle, and this method enumerates every one of them: ::: {#4696d077 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() for node in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]: g.add_node(node) g.add_edge("A", "B") g.add_edge("B", "C") g.add_edge("C", "D") g.add_edge("D", "A") g.add_edge("A", "C") trees = g.all_spanning_trees() # Returns the number of distinct spanning trees found len(trees) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#9a4bfdc4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Every tree connects all 4 nodes with exactly 3 edges [tree.count_edges() for tree in trees] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3] ``` ::: ::: **Counting Spanning Trees** A complete graph on 4 nodes (`K4`) is dense enough to have many different spanning trees -- exactly 16, matching the count predicted by Cayley's formula ($n^{n-2}$ for $n=4$): ::: {#b9f32790 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() nodes = ["A", "B", "C", "D"] for n in nodes: g.add_node(n) for i, n1 in enumerate(nodes): for n2 in nodes[i + 1:]: g.add_edge(n1, n2) trees = g.all_spanning_trees() # Returns 16 len(trees) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 16 ``` ::: ::: **Getting Edge Lists Instead of Graphs** For workloads that need to process many trees, returning raw edge lists instead of full `Graph` objects avoids the overhead of constructing a new graph for each one: ::: {#caf378a4 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_node("A") g.add_node("B") g.add_node("C") g.add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.0) g.add_edge("B", "C", weight=2.0) g.add_edge("C", "A", weight=3.0) tree_edges = g.all_spanning_trees(return_subgraphs=False) # Returns the total weight of each spanning tree [sum(w for _, _, w in edges) for edges in tree_edges] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [5.0, 4.0, 3.0] ``` ::: :::
